subject: Biology
description: Cellular respiration, ATP, photosynthesis, Krebs, Calvin

questions.stem: The energy 'currency' of the cell — used to drive most biological reactions — is:
questions.explanation: ATP — the universal immediate-energy molecule — stores energy in its phosphate bonds. When a cell needs energy, ATP → ADP + P + energy (~30 kJ/mol per bond hydrolysed). Glucose is the 'fuel', but the cell converts glucose into ATP (via respiration) because every enzyme uses ATP, not glucose, as the energy source. An average human uses ~50 kg of ATP per day (recycled many times).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Cellular respiration primarily takes place in which part of the eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria — called the 'powerhouse of the cell' (Philip Siekevitz, 1957) — carry out the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, producing most of the cell's ATP. Each mitochondrion has its own DNA (mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally). Glycolysis (the first stage) takes place in the cytoplasm. Muscle cells have thousands of mitochondria; RBCs have none.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Photosynthesis takes place in plants in the organelle called:
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts — present in plant cells and algae — contain chlorophyll and other pigments, plus the Calvin-cycle enzymes. Two parts: the thylakoids (where light reactions happen, producing ATP and NADPH) and the stroma (where the dark / Calvin reactions fix CO₂ into glucose). Chloroplasts, like mitochondria, have their own DNA — both are thought to have evolved from ancient bacterial endosymbionts.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The overall equation of photosynthesis can be summarised as:
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis — plants absorb sunlight, CO₂ and water, produce glucose and oxygen. Option A is cellular respiration (the reverse). Option C is water-formation (hydrogen burning). Option D is the Haber-Bosch ammonia-synthesis reaction. Light 'reactions' split water (releasing O₂); 'dark' Calvin reactions fix CO₂ using ATP and NADPH.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Yeast cells perform 'alcoholic fermentation' — a type of anaerobic respiration — converting glucose into:
questions.explanation: Yeast — C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH (ethanol) + 2 CO₂ + ~2 ATP. Basis of all alcoholic beverages, bread rising and bioethanol production. Animal muscle cells under low O₂ — glucose → lactic acid (NOT ethanol) + 2 ATP; this lactic-acid build-up causes post-exercise soreness. Aerobic respiration yields ~36-38 ATP from one glucose — vastly more efficient.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The primary pigment involved in capturing light energy for photosynthesis is:
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll-a is THE primary photosynthetic pigment — directly drives the light reactions. Chlorophyll-b is an accessory pigment that passes absorbed light energy to chlorophyll-a. Carotenes and xanthophylls are additional accessory pigments; they broaden the spectrum of usable light AND protect chlorophyll from photo-damage. In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down first, revealing the yellow/orange carotenoids.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The Calvin cycle, which fixes CO₂ into organic molecules, takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Calvin cycle (light-INDEPENDENT reactions, though they usually need the ATP/NADPH output of the light reactions) — takes place in the fluid-filled stroma of the chloroplast. CO₂ + RuBP (5-carbon sugar) → 3-PGA → G3P → glucose, catalysed by the famous enzyme Rubisco (the most abundant protein on Earth). Light reactions happen across the thylakoid membrane.
